newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville calmer after heavy overnight fighting.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville calmer after heavy overnight fighting.

text.p: Heavy gun and grenade fire shook the Congolese capital Brazzaville overnight despite a French announcement of a ceasefire but the city appeared calmer on Tuesday morning.
Small arms fire could still be heard from the city centre, where bodies of fighters and civilians lay unclaimed on the streets.

Automatic weapons fire and the occasional thud of a mortar resounded from other parts of town as fighting between militia followers of ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso and troops loyal to President Pascal Lissouba entered its sixth day.
A broadcast on Brazzaville's main state radio frequency on Monday night declared that Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militia controlled most of the capital.

"There was a push by Sassou's forces yesterday (Monday) and they got close to the town hall but the government forces counter-attacked and seem to have pushed them back," said Captain Alexis Jaraud, spokesman for French forces in Congo.
Jaraud told Reuters there were about 600 French troops in Brazzaville and the military hoped to fly in another 250 on Tuesday. "There are no plans at this stage to increase from 850," he said.
Jaraud said they expected more men from the 2eme REP, the Foreign Legion's Second Foreign Parachute Regiment, to reinforce the company already in Brazzaville.
Political and ethnic conflict which killed 2,000 people in the capital in 1993 exploded again as Congo approached a presidential election set for July 27.
Fighting broke out after troops surrounded Sassou Nguesso's house on Thursday morning to enforce a ban on private militias.

On Monday, French President Jacques Chirac's spokeswoman said Chirac had received agreement for a truce in telephone conversations with Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso, and they would accept mediation from Gabonese President Omar Bongo.
France, the former colonial power, has begun evacuating foreign nationals from the city. South Africa said on Tuesday French troops had helped evacuate the last of its citizens.

"The heavy weaponry that is being used, particularly multiple rocket launchers, must be causing very heavy civilian casualties but the death toll is unknown because foreign military and aid workers cannot reach many of the areas under fire," said a Western military source in Brazzaville.
He said both Lissouba's and Sassou's forces were at the airport, where there was an exchange of mortar and small arms fire on Tuesday.
The French military have to secure a section of the runway whenever a military Transall lands or takes off. Civilian flights are cancelled apart from the occasional light plane from Kinshasa.

Jaraud said the oil town of Pointe Noire was unaffected by the fighting but some people were being evacuated. An executive of Elf Acquitaine in Paris said oil production and exports were not affected.
The United States on Monday called for a ceasefire in Brazzaville and said it believed presidential elections could still be held on schedule on July 27.

Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo said a shell that landed across the river in Kinshasa from fighting in Brazzaville on Monday was a deliberate provocation. There was minimal damage when it hit the garden of a Nigerian diplomat.
